clue.text: Frank's result of Welsh pub crawl announced?

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the phrase built here is judged by how it is said

parts.note: Dai is a stereotypical Welsh man's name
after a long pub crawl you end up wrecked, very drunk
the Welshman's name and his state said together run into one word

explanation.surface: Someone asks, frankly, what happens when a Welshman goes on a pub crawl.
explanation.walkthrough: Dai is the stock Welsh name in British jokes; 'Dai wrecked' spoken quickly matches the answer. The 's is a link: Frank is the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Direct speech is candid and straightforward, a synonym of frank as an adjective.

clue.text: Transfer fee in conclusion very, very much appreciated when raised

indicators.note: in a down entry raised means lifted upward, read from bottom to top
in conclusion means at the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word
V is the standard abbreviation for very
something very much appreciated is loved

explanation.surface: A payment for a transfer is gratefully received once it has gone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very, very' looks like emphasis; the first very is just V and the second starts a phrase of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To devolve power is to transfer it down to a lower level, a synonym of hand over.

clue.text: Qualification as cowboy, say?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a condition or clause added to something
second meaning: one who rides a horse, a cowboy being an example

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what makes someone count as a cowboy; 'say' marks the cowboy as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is an added clause that qualifies a statement, and also anyone mounted on a horse.

clue.text: Influential Victorian author clearly red-pencilled

indicators.note: red-pencilled means edited or corrected, so the word before is reworked

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A major nineteenth-century writer whose work was plainly heavily edited.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish essayist and historian whose ideas shaped much Victorian thought.

clue.text: Show respect before my hound

parts.note: to bow is to show respect
'My!' and 'Wow!' are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: An instruction to bow before one's own dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow-wow is a childish or jocular word for a dog, which a hound is.

clue.text: Outrage, Beyond the Fringe?

parts.note: off means away from, beyond the limit
the end is the edge, the fringe of something

explanation.surface: Was the 1960s satirical revue Beyond the Fringe outrageous?
explanation.walkthrough: Beyond the Fringe was a famous British comedy revue; the title splits into two words of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To outrage people is to offend them deeply, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: One skilled in communication, and bagging gold medal

indicators.note: bagging means putting into a bag, so the word for and holds the others inside

parts.note: with and and both join one thing to another
or is gold in heraldry
the DSM is the Distinguished Service Medal

explanation.surface: A gifted communicator who also wins a gold medal.
explanation.definitionFit: A wordsmith is a skilled user of words, such as a writer, so expert at communicating.

clue.text: See 13 Across
Rotten scum done over, taken apart by a big gun

indicators.note: done over means done again, so the word for scum appears twice in a row

parts.note: meat or game that is high has begun to go off

indicators.note: taken apart by means split open by a letter set in between

parts.note: muck is filth, scum, here written twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: Decayed filth beaten up and torn to pieces by a powerful weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'done over' sounds like a beating but means done again; the single A then sits between the two copies.
explanation.definitionFit: High-muck-a-muck is jocular slang for a self-important person in charge, as is the idiom big gun.

clue.text: A short film full of energy

indicators.note: short means the word for a film is cut down, losing its tail

parts.note: taken as written
a video is a filmed recording

explanation.surface: A brief movie that is lively and energetic.
explanation.walkthrough: VID is the familiar clipped form of video.
explanation.definitionFit: An avid person is keen and eager, so loosely full of energy for something.

clue.text: Biodiverse area with ground on fire: cover-up by right-leaning despot?

indicators.note: a word leaning away from the right in a row of across text runs leftwards, read backwards
a cover-up wraps around something, so the ruler's title encloses the rearranged letters

parts.note: a tsar was an absolute Russian ruler

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so the two words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Burning jungle land being covered up by a politically right-wing tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right-leaning' looks political; read on the page, a word leaning away from the right runs leftwards, so the despot is reversed before it wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainforest is a dense tropical forest holding an enormous variety of plant and animal life.

clue.text: Waste, speaking when wasted?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: liquid manure or watery waste matter
second meaning, read playfully: given to slurring, as a drunk talks

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a playful coinage: a drunk slurs words, so their speech is slurry. Wasted is slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Slurry is a semi-liquid mix of farm manure or industrial residue, a type of waste.

clue.text: Don't touch German on his way around Germany

indicators.note: around says the German man's name wraps about the country's abbreviation

parts.note: Hans is a typical German man's name
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)
someone off is leaving, on their way

explanation.surface: A warning not to interfere with a German traveller heading round his country.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a command telling someone not to handle or interfere, the same as an order not to touch.

clue.text: White House club wary of far-off guarded response to ambitions

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so the preceding words are spoiled into a new order

parts.words: White House club wary of far
parts.note: all twenty-three letters are used

explanation.surface: A presidential golf club is suspicious of a distant land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'far-off' reads as one adjective, but the hyphen hides a split: far is fodder and off is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns that getting what you aspire to may bring trouble, a cautious reply to someone's hopes.

clue.text: Current art is designed on paper

indicators.note: designed means planned and arranged, so the two words before are laid out anew

parts.note: the five letters rearranged
a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: Contemporary art is planned out on paper first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective about modern art; it is a noun, a flow of air.
explanation.definitionFit: An airstream is a flow of moving air, a current in the atmosphere.

clue.text: Class warfare, I think, somewhat regressive

indicators.note: regressive means going back, so the letters run right to left
somewhat means only part of the phrase before it is wanted, a run of its letters

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of warfare and the start of think

explanation.surface: Someone's view that class conflict is a little backward-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is a rank or level, as a class is a grade within a ranked system.

clue.text: Ulcer or boil observed by one's ear?

indicators.note: judged by one's ear means taken by its spoken form rather than its spelling

parts.note: observed means saw, which in standard British speech rhymes exactly

explanation.surface: A doctor notices a skin lesion with the ear rather than the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British English, where the R is silent, saw and the answer are said the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A sore is a painful raw spot on the skin; ulcers and boils are both examples.

clue.text: Organism that is four-eyed?

indicators.note: a four-eyed person wears glasses, so the abbreviation is placed inside the spectacles

parts.note: specs is short for spectacles, worn by the four-eyed
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A question about some creature that wears glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: A species is a kind of living thing, so the word loosely stands for a type of organism.

clue.text: Slightly off, s-scent of gardens?

parts.note: the stammered opening letter is taken as written
Kew Gardens is the Royal Botanic Gardens in west London
a whiff is a faint smell

explanation.surface: Someone stammers that a garden's smell is not quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter supplies a spare S; then 'scent of gardens' gives a Kew smell, the gardens coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: Skew-whiff is British slang for askew or crooked, meaning not quite straight or right.

clue.text: See 13 Across
Blow hot dish

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to waste or squander money, to blow it
second meaning: a piece of food fried in batter

explanation.walkthrough: Blow looks like a punch or gust, but it is slang for squandering; the matching verb is used with 'away'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fritter money is to waste it, and a fritter is also a fried battered food served hot.

clue.text: Cue in slang I screwed up

indicators.note: screwed up means crumpled and mangled, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged; that they also run backwards across these words is a coincidence

explanation.surface: An actor's prompt in street talk that the speaker botched.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is a prompt to act, which is what a signal gives.

clue.text: Money bound to inspire premier in surprisingly moderate policy

parts.note: a cent is a small coin

indicators.note: to inspire is to breathe in, so the boundary word takes a letter inside it

parts.note: a rim is a boundary or edge

indicators.note: premier means first, so only the leading letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Cash is certain to motivate a prime minister, astonishingly, toward middle-of-the-road politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to' looks like 'certain to'; bound is really a noun for an edge, and 'to inspire' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Centrism is a political stance in the middle ground, avoiding the extremes of left and right.

clue.text: Overheard, a beautiful thing

indicators.note: overheard means caught by listening, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: taken as written
fair is an old word for beautiful
the two words said together

explanation.surface: Someone eavesdropping hears a lovely object described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a beautiful thing' looks like the whole description, but thing is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a thing with someone means a romantic fling, and an affair is such a relationship.

clue.text: Great passion consuming sweets after a turnover?

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so the emotion holds the other piece inside

parts.note: fire is ardour, passion

indicators.note: a turnover flips something, so the word for sweets is read backwards

parts.note: tarts are sweet pastries

explanation.surface: A tremendous lust for cakes following a fruit pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: A turnover is also a folded fruit pastry, which suits the sweets in the surface; here it only means flipping a word over.
explanation.definitionFit: First-rate means of the highest quality, excellent, as great does in praise.

clue.text: Sycophantic luvvy ultimately backing Yankee in Jolie?

indicators.note: in places the letter for the phonetic code word inside the French term

parts.note: jolie is French for nice, which said in the city of Nice gives Nice nice
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A gushing actor finally supports an American appearing alongside Angelina Jolie.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul's joke: jolie means nice in French, and in the French city of Nice it is 'Nice nice'. Y goes in the middle and luvvy's last letter is backing it, at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicey-nicey describes cloyingly pleasant behaviour put on to please, the manner of a flatterer.

clue.text: See 23 Down
Just monkey caught by foxy

indicators.note: something caught by another is held inside it

parts.note: foxy means cunning, sly
a mischievous child is a monkey, or an imp

explanation.surface: Nothing more than an ape seized by a cunning fox.
explanation.definitionFit: Simply and just are both adverbs meaning merely, as in 'just a minute'.

clue.text: Originally clinker-built, say, sailing ship

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: A boat built from overlapping planks, so to speak, is a type of sailing vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Clinker-built describes a hull of overlapping planks, so the surface sounds like boatbuilding.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutter is a small single-masted sailing vessel, a type of sailing ship.
